ARC: The Fall of Baekje (660–661)

=== EPISODE 72: Yellow Mountain (660)
## Snow on the Steppe
Three years before he sees Samhan, Su Dingfang wins a war in a blizzard. He is sixty-five. His enemy has camped for the winter, sure that nobody fights in snow two feet deep. Su marches all night and attacks at dawn. He takes the whole camp before anyone in it has found his boots.
sudingfang: Snow is just cold sand. / Nobody expects you in it. That’s the only good thing about it.
He comes home with the qaghan in a cart and a red banner over his own tent, a bird with its wings spread, painted by a regiment that had decided he needed one. Chang’an is calling him the Red Fowl long before anyone official does.
## Deokmul Island
That summer he sails east with a hundred and thirty thousand men and anchors off a small island. A hundred Silla ships come out to meet him. At their head is the crown prince, Bupmin. He is thirty-four, and trying not to stare at the size of the Tang flagship.
sudingfang: You’re the son?
munmu: Kim Bupmin, General. My father the king sends his—
sudingfang: Tenth day of the seventh month. South of Sabi. Your army and mine, on the same field, on the same morning. / Tell your father. Tell him twice.
munmu: We will be there, General.
Bupmin is rowed back to his own ship. Behind him the Red Fowl says something to his staff that makes them laugh.
sudingfang: They’ll be late. Small countries always are. They have to ask too many uncles.
## Geumdol Fortress
The king rides as far as a hill fort and no farther. The field belongs to his son and to Yushin. Fifty thousand men march west with a date in their heads. Between them and the date is the pass at Tanhyeon. Beyond the pass is a man called Gyebek.
chunchu: The tenth day, then. / …Yushin. Don’t let the Tang get there first. They’ll write it down that way for a thousand years.
## Gibeolpo
On the ninth day, the Tang fleet sails into the river mouth at Gibeolpo. The shore there is a mile of grey mud. Baekje’s soldiers wait on the high ground. They watch the first Tang companies wade in up to the thigh.
sudingfang: Mud is just wet road. / Give it something to hold.
His men lay willow mats on the mud, one after another, a road made of baskets, and the army walks across it dry-shod. By evening the Baekje line is broken and the river is open to Sabi.
The same morning, forty miles east, the Silla army comes down out of the hills onto the Yellow Mountain Fields, and finds five thousand men already standing in its way.
## Yellow Mountain Fields
Hundred-Victories gets to the Yellow Mountain Fields first and picks his ground. Then he waits — for the Sword of Silla, or for arithmetic, whichever arrives with a banner. Yellow lacquer holds the palisade. When the Sword arrives it is a tall black helm and a blue rim. The tall Silla helm comes in at a gallop. They meet in the dust. Blue plume cuts yellow lacquer.
He sets three camps across the three ways in. There is no fourth way in; that is why he chose the place.
He walked the ground for two days before choosing it, in the same direction each time, and he can still tell you the number of paces between the eastern camp and the stream.
gyebek: Four hundred and twelve.
gyebek: …Nobody asked. I know.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 47, Biographies — Gyebek; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 2, p. 452] With the men of one country I face the great armies of Tang and Silla, and whether the country lives or dies cannot be known. I fear my wife and children will be taken and made slaves. Compared with living in disgrace, a swift death is better.
gyebek: And theirs?
gyebek: Fifty thousand, my lord.
gyebek: Five thousand against fifty thousand….
Then the air above the Yellow Mountain does what air should not. Kangrim hangs there in plain day — visible not to one dying man but to all five thousand at once. They have already finished negotiating with life.
They cheer. They wave. Someone shouts a greeting as if King Yumla’s escort were a popular general arriving late to his own war. Kangrim, who has collected kings with less fuss for His Majesty, actually blinks.
kangrim: …You can all see me. / That is — new. / Ah. You have already decided. Of course.
kangrim: General. The five thousand can already see me — so I will ask you alone. / When you killed your family to keep your oath: was that loyalty, or terror of becoming soft?
gyebek: …Loyalty. / If it was terror, do not tell them. Let them keep the prettier word.
gyebek: Men of Baekje — / If even death showed up early, we must be on time. / Spears.
Gyebek kneels. He plants the phoenix ring in the yellow dust and keeps his hand on it. Gyebek stands when the dust has learned the shape.
Five thousand against fifty thousand — not a formation so much as a sentence written in bodies. Like the three hundred at Thermopylae in stories that have not yet reached Samhan, they arrange themselves to be remembered rather than rescued. The math does not change. The watching does.
Seventh-month heat sits on the Yellow Mountain like a second army. Dust rises white off the three roads. Downstream, Tang sails already crowd the river mouth. They are waiting for the inland door to open. This field is that door.
gyebek: Long ago Goujian of the Central Plain shattered Wu’s host of seven hundred thousand with five thousand men. Today let each of us fight with all his strength, and repay the country’s grace with victory.
yushin: So — you are this Hundred-Victories Gyebek I have heard of? / The taverns still split the Greatest Blade of Samhan between us. Shall we settle their argument?
gyebek: Then you must be the Sword of the Divine Country. / I do not drink in taverns. I count. Today the count is five against fifty — and titles after.
yushin: Fifty thousand is a number. / Five thousand that already waved at death is another kind of number. / Hold your ground, then. We will come and measure it.
## The First Clash
Silla comes on the first time in three columns: Yushin centre, Heumsun left, Pumil right. Down the three roads at once, exactly as the arithmetic says. Uphill. In the heat. Into yellow shields set edge to edge. The archers wait to see which column is thickest, and loose at that one. All three camps throw them back into their own dust.
gyebek: One.
## The Second Clash
The second time Silla does not spread itself across three roads. It comes down the northern road in one fist at the left camp, hwarang in front, on the theory that the camp which shot the most is the camp with the fewest arrows left. It is a good theory. The left camp has counted its arrows too, and has been shooting half of what it could. The fist opens on the stakes and goes back up the road carrying its own.
gyebek: Two.
gyebek: Report.
gyebek: …Left camp still has arrows. / Centre has men. / Right has both, and less of each than an hour ago.
## The Third Clash
The third time Pumil takes the southern road, where the ground is softest and the right camp sits lowest, and for the length of a held breath the right road almost opens — and closes again on spears counted in the night. The camp is not quite where Pumil’s scouts drew it at dawn. It is further back and higher, every pace of the difference is uphill, and the Silla line arrives at the stakes with nothing left in its legs.
gyebek: Three.
## The Fourth Clash
The fourth time Yushin rides at the head of the centre himself, on the white horse, and meets Hundred-Victories in the gap between the camps. Both armies stop to watch two men, which armies are not supposed to do. It lasts about as long as it takes a banner to fall and be picked up again, and then the white horse is going back the way it came with a red line along its shoulder, and the Sword of Silla is holding his left arm against his ribs.
Behind him the fifty thousand sit down where they stand. Four times up the same slope in the same heat — the clerks will write that the soldiers’ strength was spent, which is the polite way to say that grown men are lying in the dust of their own road and cannot be made to get up.
gyebek: Four.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 5, Silla Annals — King Muyeol, year 7] Yushin and the others divided the army into three roads. They fought four times without advantage, and the soldiers’ strength was spent.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 28, Baekje Annals — King Uija, year 20] He led five thousand men sworn to die out to Hwangsan and fought the Silla army. Four times they met, and four times he won; but his men were few and his strength gave out, and at last he was defeated. Gyebaek died there.
Both kingdoms wrote the morning down. They agree on the number, and on nothing else.
After the fourth time there is a lull, the kind both sides pretend is for water. Yushin rides out alone into the gap on the white horse, his sleeve tied off with his own sash, and stops at a distance where a bow would be bad manners. After a while the black horse comes out of the centre camp to meet him. Nobody is near enough to hear. The chronicle has it anyway, the way it has most things, from men who swore afterwards they had not been listening.
Black horse, white horse, nose to nose in the yellow dust. From either line they look like a pair of go stones someone has forgotten to play.
yushin: Your right camp. You moved it in the night.
gyebek: Forty paces. / …You noticed.
yushin: On the third time. Not before. / …How old are you.
gyebek: Forty. Near enough. Nobody wrote it down.
yushin: Sixty-five. / If we had met when I was forty, I would have had you. / …No. I would not have.
Gyebek looks at the tied sleeve and does not say anything polite about it.
gyebek: You came yourself, the fourth time. You did not have to.
yushin: The boys needed to see it could be done.
gyebek: Could it?
yushin: Not by me. Not today. / I came with fifty thousand. I still have forty-some. You came with five.
gyebek: Four. Now.
yushin: I know. I can count too.
gyebek: Then go home.
yushin: You first.
Neither of them laughs, but it is close.
gyebek: Your taverns.
yushin: What about them.
gyebek: Nothing. They will have a long winter.
They turn the horses at the same moment, black and white, as if somebody had rehearsed it, and ride back to their counts. In the Silla line Heumsun is already looking at his son.
The hwarang yard still tells its oldest story in two names: two boys who swore, and did not outlive the swear. Nobody here says the rhyme aloud. The field supplies it anyway. Bangul rides first. Gwanchang rides second.
## Bangul & Gwanchang
Heumsun calls his son to his stirrup. Bangul is fifteen, near enough, and Yushin’s nephew; he comes at a run, because he has been watching his father look at him since the white horse came back.
?: For a subject, nothing is greater than loyalty. For a son, nothing is greater than filial piety. / To see the danger and give your life to it — that keeps both, whole, at once.
bangul: I have heard you, Father.
Bangul rides out alone and does not come back. He goes into the Baekje line where it is thickest and fights there until it closes over him, and the place where it closed is the place Silla aims at next.
Pumil does not call his son. He has him brought to stand in front of his horse, before all the generals, and points at him the way a man points at a map.
pumil: My son is only sixteen, but his spirit is brave enough. / In today’s battle — can he be the mark the three armies aim by?
gwanchang: Yes.
He takes an armoured horse and one spear and goes straight at the Baekje centre. He gets further than Bangul did. Then they pull him off the horse alive and bring him to Gyebek.
Gyebek has the helmet taken off. Inside it is a boy’s face, sweat-striped, furious at being alive.
gyebek: Silla cannot be withstood. / If a boy is like this — what are its grown men? / Go home.
They put him back on his horse and point it at the Silla line. At his father’s stirrup Gwanchang does not get down.
gwanchang: I went into their midst and could not cut down their general or take their banner. / It was not because I was afraid to die.
Behind the Silla line there is a well, dug that morning for the horses. He scoops the water out with both hands, drinks, and rides back the way he came. Gyebek sends him home once. He comes back.
The second time, Gyebek has his helmet unstrapped again, looks at the face inside it for a while, and then does what he has to. He ties the head to the saddle and sends the horse back.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 47, Biographies — Gwanchang; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 2, p. 454] Gyebaek cut off his head, tied it to the saddle, and sent it back. Pumil took up the head and said: my son’s face is as if he lived. He was able to die in the king’s service; I have nothing to regret.
He holds the head up in front of the army and wipes the blood from its face with his own sleeve, so that the three armies can see whose son it is.
## The Fifth Clash · The Final Stand
Nobody gives an order. The drums start on their own, one column and then the next, and fifty thousand men who could not be made to get up an hour ago are on their feet and shouting.
The Silla line, which has failed four times that morning, goes forward and does not stop. A father’s wet sleeve is worth more than a fourth failure. The left camp goes under first — not broken so much as used up. The right holds one more breath, then folds toward the centre like a hinge that has decided to finish.
On the Baekje side, nobody says five.
By the fifth charge the left camp is a rumour of men. Gyebek’s centre is the last grammar the field still understands — a thin line of Baekje that refuses to become a paragraph about surrender. Spears shorten. Names stop answering. Kangrim, who has been hanging in the day like unfinished weather, comes down to speaking distance.
He reads the general's name three times across the field — Gyebek. Gyebek. Gyebek. — though five thousand throats have already answered.
kangrim: General. / Your five thousand already waved. / I only ask what I asked: loyalty, or terror of becoming soft?
gyebek: …Loyalty. I said it. / And you — you were heaven’s messenger. / Sent to arrest King Yumla. You stayed. A crow mixed the pages of your ledger. / That is why nobody knows their hour until you are already in the room.
kangrim: … / The island told you. / Living men are not supposed to finish that sentence. / How long have you been carrying my origin like a spare spear?
gyebek: Five years of evenings on Tamla. / They save your story for last — after every kinder tale. / I counted the stories the way I count paces. / When you hung above us this morning, I already knew which kingdom’s marshal you were.
kangrim: Surprise is rare in my work. / Thank you for that — His Majesty appreciates accurate minutes.
[FLASHBACK 632 I will complete my duty]
  A nameless boy at the White River, newly called Gyebek, answers a prince the only way he knows.
  gyebek: I will complete my duty.
  euija: …Good. / That is a sharper vow than most crowns get.
The field returns. The vow has come due.
gyebek: Your Majesty… I have completed my duty.
Kangrim, who has been hanging in the day like unfinished weather, closes the distance.
kangrim: Walk, then. The underworld kingdom keeps better hours than Sabi ever did.
The man who counted everything finishes counting, and walks. The Yellow Mountain keeps the dust. The White River, downstream, opens.
The Silla clerks count too. Twenty-odd taken alive, two ministers among them. Nobody writes down how many of the five thousand were left to take.
Nobody can lead the black horse off the field. It stands over the place where he went down until the Silla grooms come at dusk with ropes, and it takes six of them, and in the night it breaks the line and goes south toward the ferry it was named for. Nobody on either side ever reports seeing it again.
gaozong: ?
The pass is open. The river is open. And in Sabi, the king’s big idea is to send the Tang dinner…!

=== EPISODE 73: Sabi (660)
The court hears about the Yellow Mountain Fields the following morning.
Euija’s first move is to send the Tang camp a feast: oxen, wine, three cartloads of rice cakes. The court is told this is diplomacy.
euija: Nobody burns a city on a full stomach. / Feed them. Then we’ll talk about what they want.
The oxen come back that afternoon, untouched, with the drovers walking behind them.
## The Red Fowl’s Tent
The Silla army reaches the Tang camp two days late. The Red Fowl has the Silla supply officer dragged to his tent gate. They open his collar for the sword.
sudingfang: The tenth day. South of Sabi. I said it twice. / Take his head. Then we can start.
Kim Yushin walks into the tent with a battle-axe in his hand.
yushin: The general did not see the Yellow Mountain Fields. / If you mean to punish us for being late, I will not be shamed for a crime I did not commit. I will fight the Tang first, and Baekje after.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 5, Silla Annals — King Muyeol, yr. 7 (660), seventh month] Then he stood at the camp gate leaning on his axe; his angry hair stood up like planted stakes, and the precious sword at his waist leapt of itself from its scabbard.
The Red Fowl’s second-in-command steps on his commander’s foot.
Dong Baoliang: (low) The Silla army is about to turn on us, General.
Kim Munyeong’s collar is closed again. Nobody in the tent mentions the date for the rest of the war.
Euija leaves Sabi at night for Bear Fortress, with fewer men than he expected to have.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 28, Baekje Annals — King Uija, yr. 20 (660); Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 386] The king knew he could not escape, and sighed: I regret that I did not use Seongchung’s words, and have come to this.
euija: Kim Chunchu… / KIM CHUNCHU!!!
chunchu: Hm?
euija: Kim Chunchu, you wretch!! / You vile traitor of the ages, who dragged a foreign power onto the soil of Samhan!! / Heaven’s punishment will find you!!
Euija’s second son, left behind, crowns himself the next morning. A grandson takes one look at the Tang camp and does the sum. An uncle who stays will kill whoever opens the gate. So the grandson climbs down the wall on a rope with his household. Half the city follows him down it.
The crown prince comes out of the gate. Chunbok walks a careful pace behind him. Bupmin has the prince knelt in the dirt before his horse, and spits in his face.
munmu: Long ago your father had my younger sister killed unjustly and buried in a prison. That deed left my heart sore and my head aching for twenty years — and today your life is in my hands!
Yung lies flat on the ground and says nothing.
chunbok: As the generals will surely appreciate, the gate was opened for the sake of the people, and in full accordance with—
## Falling Flower Rock
When the gate opens the palace women do not wait to be counted. They go out the back of the palace and up the ridge path to the cliff above the White River, where the rock drops straight into the water, and the soldiers coming up behind them find nobody at the top.
The stories that gave Euija three thousand women give them this cliff as well, and three thousand is the number they say went over it, their skirts opening on the way down like petals. That is why the rock is called Nakhwaam, the Rock of Falling Flowers. Nobody who was there wrote down how many it really was. There was no one left on the cliff to count.
## Ungjin
Bear Fortress belongs to the king the way a borrowed house belongs to a guest. The Ye family has held it for four generations. Ye Sikjin gives the king his own rooms, and goes up on the wall every morning to count the Tang sails on the river.
euija: Sikjin! Good man. Your grandfather held this rock for my grandfather, eh? / We’ll hold it again. The Red Fowl can’t sit in the mud forever.
yesikjin: My grandfather held it, Majesty. / …For whoever was king.
On the fifth night he comes into the king’s rooms with his brother and twenty men, and the king understands before anyone speaks.
By morning the king is on his way to the Red Fowl’s tent.
[QUOTE Jiu Tangshu (舊唐書) bk. 83, Biography of Su Dingfang] Its great general Ye Sik also brought Uija and came to surrender.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 28, Baekje Annals — King Uija, yr. 20 (660); Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 386] Thereupon the king and Crown Prince Hyo, together with the several fortresses, all surrendered.
Nobody counts them. Nobody has counted them for years. It had been two, once, and a joke, and a modest number a man was proud of.
courtmaid: He’ll reach for us today, like yesterday.
courtmaid: He isn’t here today. / …But the body remembers.
The rock is called the Falling Flowers afterwards, which is a kind way of saying it, and Baekje’s last invention.
Chunchu finally arrives at the scene. He makes Euija pour his wine, and the Tang general’s beside it. Then he settles an old debt. Gumil, the man who opened his daughter’s gate, is put to death.
chunchu: So… you are Euija. / The one who started all of this… Buyeo Euija. / Do you know what it cost me to bring you in? / Nearly my whole life, you bastard.
A cup is put into Euija’s hands, and he is made to pour.
euija: …Do you know what I said to Gesomun, once. / “I do not fear a man who kneels to another man.”
chunchu: I know. / I was the man he said it about.
euija: …And so — who is kneeling today?
euija: Chunchu… / One day you will kneel before someone too.
chunchu: Take this man away.
## The Pagoda
A month later the Tang carve their victory into a stone pagoda. They put it low, where anyone walking round has to read it. It calls the conquest a deliverance. About Baekje’s king it says:
[QUOTE Datang ping Baekje guo beiming (大唐平百濟國碑銘), carved on the five-storey stone pagoda of Jeongnimsa, Buyeo (660)] Abroad he cast off his upright ministers; at home he trusted a bewitching woman.
chunchu: Harmonized.
Then the Tang divide Baekje into five commanderies, with a Tang governor over each and Baekje men under them. Nothing in the arrangement is labelled Silla.
munmu: Father. Everything south of Pyongyang and the whole of Baekje. He said it in front of the horses. You told me.
chunchu: I did. / He also said an emperor’s word was the writing. I should have brought a brush.
In the Tang lines the Red Fowl’s staff officers are seen pacing out the distance to the Silla camp, which is not a thing allies measure. In the Silla council a man proposes that their soldiers put on Baekje clothes and fall on the Tang by night.
yushin: A dog fears its master, Majesty. / But step on its foot and it bites. Even a dog knows that much.
Word of the conversation reaches the Red Fowl’s tent, as it was meant to.
A month later the Red Fowl sails home with Euija, his sons and twelve thousand captives. He leaves ten thousand men to hold the city. Beside them sits a Silla army that has stopped smiling.
Across the sea, a confession is waiting for Euija. It is already written, in a lovely hand. It only needs his name…!

=== EPISODE 74: Buyeo Euija† (660)
In the Tang capital, Euija is brought forth before the Third Emperor.
First, paperwork. A palace clerk hands the prisoner a confession, already written out in a fair hand. There is a space at the bottom for his name.
Tang clerk: Aloud, please. Clearly. The scribes are taking it down.
euija: ‘I, the criminal Euija, having been liberated by the Great Tang—’ / Liberated. Hm. So that’s what that was. / ‘—confess with gratitude that without the Great Tang there would be no New Baekje—’ / There isn’t one. You burned it. / ‘—and resolve to serve the Emperor for ten thousand years.’ / Ten thousand? I’m sixty. Ambitious fellow, your clerk.
euija: It’s a bad story. Nobody’s afraid of anything, there’s no villain, and the hero is a building. / Who wrote this? I’ve done better drunk.
Tang clerk: Your name, please. Here.
He signs in a hand so large the name runs off the edge of the paper, and gives it back. The clerk files it without looking. A confession only needs a name, and has never much minded whose.
Afterwards the emperor asks his general a question in front of the whole court.
gaozong: You were there with an army. Why didn’t you take Silla while you were at it?
sudingfang: Their king is kind and loves his people. His ministers serve the country loyally. Below, they serve those above like fathers and elder brothers. / It is a small country, Majesty. But it cannot be schemed against.
euija: Kim Chunchu… / KIM CHUNCHU!!!
Across the sea, in Surabol, King Muyeol is eating his supper.
chunchu: Hm?
euija: Kim Chunchu, you wretch!! / You vile traitor of the ages, who dragged a foreign power onto the soil of Samhan!! / Heaven’s punishment will find you!!
The shouting burns out. What remains is a man who has finally run out of stories to sell — and one last story he cannot afford to keep.
euija: Let someone… avenge me…! / Let someone… raise Baekje again…! / Chunchu — what you finished… may it never stay finished…!
He is shouting at the man who won. Later men will call it Later Baekje, put a different crown on it, and argue whether the name counts.
euija: Heh… so you guys are real after all…
haewonmek: Any last words?
Euija waits. He has always been good at making a room lean in.
euija: No.
Kangrim reads his name three times in the Tang capital — Euija. Euija. Euija. — the underworld's receipt before the humiliation finishes.
kangrim: Eraha. / The boy at the White River. The name you gave him is still in the ledger.
euija: …A friend. / Put the miracle on the cheap side of the page.
kangrim: Then you die richer than the record will admit. / Come.
Euija dies, vengeful and emptied. His life flashes before his eyes.
He was the bright prince once. Then the conqueror. Now he is a man in his enemy’s capital with nothing left to command.
He pleads for someone, maybe in future generations, to finally avenge him.
Somewhere far down the years, a stranger is already reaching for his banner.
Thus was the end of Buyeo Euija.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 28, Baekje Annals — King Uija, accession notice; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 380 · cf. Jiu Tangshu (舊唐書) bk. 199上, Baekje] He served his parents with filial piety and treated his brothers with fraternal love; in his time he was called the Zengzi of the East of the Sea.
A man the court once called the Zengzi of the East.
— Buyeo Euija —
He was right about everything, which is the particular cruelty of his case. A country is a story. He said so at forty-one, in a courtyard, to a boy he had named himself.
And then he learned the rest of it, which he had not thought about: that a story does not care who is telling it. That the moment you make yourself its author you have also made yourself a character in it, and characters can be revised.
He broke the eight clans because they were strangling the throne, and he was correct. He seated his own sons instead, and was correct again — and then found himself alone in a room where every voice agreed with him — a room that had stopped being a court some years earlier, and become a mirror.
Seongchung told him. He put Seongchung in a cell. Heungsu told him. He had already exiled Heungsu. Gyebek would have told him, and he had put Gyebek on a boat. A man does not fall because nobody warned him. He falls because he arranged, patiently and over years, to be somewhere the warnings could not reach.
The Zengzi of the East. They called him that when he was young, and they meant it. The name was neither flattery nor wrong. He was never a fool. He was a clever man who won, and kept winning, until winning was the only instrument he had left, and then he tried to play a dying country on it.
He asked, at the end, for someone to avenge him. Two hundred and forty years later a man called Kyun Hwon raised his banner and used his name and lost as well. The story went on without either of them. It always does.
Baekje is gone. Goguryeo still stands. And the man who arranged both can no longer get out of bed…?

=== EPISODE 75: Kim Chunchu† (661)
They take him first to a Buddhist temple on the edge of Surabol — not for miracle, for quiet. Incense. Stone. A monk who knows when not to speak. Munhee sits where wives of True Bone have always sat when history arrives as a fever.
munhee: You reinvented a kingdom in a side hall. / Leave me the hours. I invent endings.
It is the sixth month of 661. Baekje has fallen, Goguryeo has not, and the man who arranged both is fifty-eight and cannot get out of bed.
Munhee (55) sits where she has sat since the spring. She has buried a sister who was a queen and a brother’s youth and a daughter she never got back, and she is still here — until their son comes and stands at the foot of the bed, already wearing a king’s silence he has not yet been allowed to begin.
chunchu: Munhee. Have I… paid all of it?
munhee: Not yet. I’ll pay the rest.
He looks past her, to the boy who is no longer a boy. Bupmin (35) has his mother’s stillness and his father’s hunger, and for a moment the room holds all three of them the way a hill once held a promise.
chunchu: Bupmin.
munmu: Father.
chunchu: People will say… this whole war was only for your sister. / Gotaso. / And they will not be wrong. Daeya never left this room for a single day.
chunchu: But that was never the only bill I was paying. / What you used to say when you were small. When the word still sat wrong in your mouth. / “A king for all.” / Not a king of Silla. Of everyone.
munmu: That was… your dream first, Father. / On the hill, with Uncle—
chunchu: I said it first. You took it. / That is how children steal. They take the largest thing in the room. / I cleared the road as far as Baekje. Goguryeo is still standing, and the Tang will be smiling. / The rest — walk it as king. / Not as my revenge. As the country you wanted when you were six.
munmu: …I promise.
chunchu: Bupmin… I love you.
The escort arrives on schedule.
He reads the king's name three times — Muyeol. Muyeol. Muyeol. — though the room still knows him as Chunchu.
He goes quiet between the two names. The room still knows him as Chunchu. The ledger has already written Muyeol.
kangrim: King Muyeol. / We have met before — in your daughter’s eyes, if not in yours. / Your son is packing. The West is already in the hall.
chunchu: …I know. / I saw a room where they all absolutely obeyed one man — no matter what. / I never un-saw it. Tell Bupmin the packing list is his.
chunchu: I am… just going to keep walking west.
kangrim: The ledger does not moralize — His Majesty only asks whether you knew. You knew. / Walk, Spring-and-Autumn. The underworld kingdom has a seat that keeps better silence than Chang’an.
King Muyeol (58) dies.
Twelve years earlier an emperor had told him that Goguryeo was the one failure of his life, and that Baekje would be Chunchu’s. Only one of them was wrong.
They give him a name for the dead: Muyeol. His temple name borrows the Second Emperor’s two characters. He was the first True Bone king ever crowned. He will be the last man anyone calls a diplomat.
— Kim Chunchu —
He was a boy on a hill who wanted one country and no more borders, and he got half of it, and left the rest in his son’s mouth — the same words, stolen honestly, when the boy was still small enough to believe a king could be for everyone.
First the politics, which he gave up for a wife and three children. Then the wife and the children, one of whom was taken from him at Daeya, which gave the politics back to him with interest. He did not choose the second time. That is what people never understand about him.
He knelt to Gesomun, who despised him for it. He knelt to an emperor, who liked him for it and kept his son. Euija said he did not fear a man who kneels. Euija was wrong. It took eighteen years and a cup of wine to show him.
The charge against him is that he brought a foreign army onto Samhan soil, and the charge is true. He knew it while he was doing it. He did it anyway, and spent the rest of his life teaching his son how to get them out again.
He died with Baekje gone and Goguryeo still standing. Halfway. The last two names he said were his daughter’s and his son’s. Not the kingdom’s.
Bupmin takes the throne. They will call him Munmu. He vows to finish it, for the country a six-year-old once named out loud.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 6, Silla Annals — King Munmu, accession (661); Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 140] King Munmu was set up. His taboo-name was Beopmin; he was the eldest son of King Taejong.
Silla won the war. So why does the emperor’s new edict call its king a clerk…?

=== EPISODE 76: Ungjin Commandery (661)
## Five Commanderies
When the capital fell, the Tang threw five commanderies over the country like a net over a pond. The biggest knot sits at Bear Fortress, where Euija was handed over. So far the net catches mostly rebels.
## The Black Tortoise
That spring a new man takes over the Tang garrison. Nobody in Chang’an expected to see him in uniform again. Liu Rengui is sixty. Last year he lost a grain fleet in a storm and was stripped of office. Now he comes east as a commoner in white, to earn it back. In his baggage: the Tang calendar, and the list of names nobody may write.
liurengui: Heaven means to make an old man rich, it seems. / Send me the calendar for this country, and the list of names one must not write. If we are going to sweep the east clean, the east should at least know what year it is.
The rebels come and go like weather, and between storms the Black Tortoise does what he actually came for, which is paperwork. He counts the households of Baekje village by village and writes them down as numbers. He mends dykes and bridges. He posts the Tang calendar at every crossroads, with the list of names that may not be written, so that the people of Baekje will know which characters to leave out of their letters home.
liurengui: A village that knows what year it is pays its tax on time. / Put one up at the ferry as well. People read while they wait for the boat.
## Gyerim
Then an edict arrives for the new king. It makes him Grand Commander of the Gyerim Prefecture. Gyerim is his country’s oldest name, the wood where a rooster crowed over a golden box. In the edict it is one province of the empire. And the king is its governor.
munmu: A prefecture, Uncle. They have made my father’s country into a prefecture, and me its clerk.
yushin: Then sign as its clerk, Majesty. / And keep a copy.
The court is angrier than the king. Men in the Council hall who have not agreed on anything since the old queen died agree that a prefecture is an insult, and say so loudly, in rooms where no Tang officer is present.
daeto: They’re not wrong about everything, you know. / Have you seen their calendar? Every day accounted for. Our almanac can’t even agree with itself about the solstice.
Nobody answers him. A few men remember afterwards that he said it.
## Chang’an
In Chang’an the Third Emperor is told that Baekje is finished and that its king has died in the capital of a broken heart, and he takes out his father’s maps.
gaozong: Father went east three times and came home coughing. / Baekje was the knife at Goguryeo’s back, and now we’re holding it — no. That sounds like something he would say. Write it down anyway.
wuzetian: Then don’t say it like him. Say it like you. / Four generals. One for each side of the map, so none of them can come home claiming he did it alone.
That is how the Four Beasts are chosen: by a woman who knows how generals talk at banquets.
## The Four Beasts
The Third Emperor launches the Eighth Invasion of Goguryeo — his father’s war, inherited along with everything else.
[diagram four-beasts]
[diagram four-dragons]
Samhan never learns their names. It learns their banners, which is the entire purpose of a banner.
gaozong: I have already destroyed Baekje and removed your country’s worry; yet now Goryeo trusts in the ruggedness of its land, joins the Yemaek in wickedness, breaks the rite of serving a great state, and abandons the duty of living peaceably with its neighbours. I am sending soldiers to strike it — so return and tell your king to send out his army, and with us annihilate these failing barbarians.
Baekje has no king. Across the sea, an exiled prince is packing his bags…!

=== EPISODE 77: King Pungjang (661)
[FLASHBACK 371 The Seven-Branched Sword]
  A Baekje king sends the King of Wa a sword with seven branches. It is a gift. It is also a message.
  Baekje–Wa relations continue to flourish and Wang In spreads western literature to the Yamato kingdom.
  It is iron, two and a half feet long, with six branches off a central blade and sixty-one characters inlaid in gold down both sides. It has never been sharpened. It was never going to be.
  The inscription is the interesting part, because the two countries have spent fifteen hundred years disagreeing about a single verb: whether Baekje presented it upward, or bestowed it downward.
  herald: Which is it?
  herald: That depends on which country is doing the reading.
  What is not in dispute: Baekje sent scholars, craftsmen, weavers, horse-handlers, potters and the written word across that water for three hundred years, and when Baekje finally needed ships, the East sent forty-two thousand men to die in a river for it.
  Whichever verb it was, it was paid.
Gwishil Boksin sends to Yamato the East with a hundred Tang prisoners as a present, and asks for two things: an army, and Prince Pung, who has lived there for twenty years.
[diagram restoration-army]
[FLASHBACK 660 Asuka, that winter]
  Asuka, the tenth month. The Baekje envoy has come the whole way with frost in his beard and a hundred Tang soldiers roped neck to neck behind him, a present, which is a polite word for proof. The empress is sixty-six. She has buried two husbands, held this throne twice and sat through a great many envoys, and she lets this one finish.
  tenji: A hundred prisoners. Generous. / …That’s the first page, though. When do they show us the rest of the bill?
  The envoy tells him. Soldiers, and the prince. Every head in the hall turns to the prince, who has lived in this palace for twenty years and who discovers that he has been sitting very straight.
  abe: Send me! I’ve crossed the cold sea. / I’ve taken Mishihase arrows. The western sea’s only warmer. I’ll bring you back their emperor’s hat!
  tenji: Before anyone asks him anything, Mother, I will. / Prince. Do they want you, or your name?
  pung: …Both, I expect. The name first. / I am still a son of Baekje. I have only… forgotten some of the words.
  The empress has let all of it run: her son’s arithmetic, the admiral’s hat, the prince’s missing words. Then she speaks once.
  saimei: Asking for soldiers is old. Holding up a falling house is older. / The sea is also a border, my son. When the western roof catches, our eaves are next. / Give them the ships. Give the boy a cap of rank and a wife, so he does not arrive looking like a hostage.
  [QUOTE Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) vol. 26, Empress Saimei 6 (660), 10th month — the edict to aid Baekje] To beg for troops and plead for rescue, this we have heard of from of old; to steady the falling and continue the severed line is written in the constant laws. …… Gather like clouds and move like thunder, assemble together at Sataku, cut down its whales and loosen those who hang upside down.
  Abe is out of the hall before the edict is copied. The prince goes to find a tailor. The eastern prince, who agrees with his mother on everything she has decided, writes the cost of it down on a separate sheet anyway.
The eastern empress raises ships, grain and soldiers for the restoration.
She dies the next year. Her son takes the throne and keeps her promise. Baekje's refugees start coming home from everywhere they ran.
## Roll Call
Juryu, the ninth month of 661. Prince Pung comes ashore below the fortress with a cap of rank, a Yamato wife, five thousand eastern soldiers and an admiral nobody asked for, and finds the founders of the restoration drawn up on the shingle to meet him. Boksin has written the order of introductions on a tally board. He has made them rehearse it twice.
The board begins with Boksin. The order lasts until Abe no Hirafu, who is not on it, leaps from the gunwale of the first boat into surf up to his knees, flings his arms wide in his wolf-fur and his red cape, and introduces himself to the fortress, the gulls and the Tang scouts on the far ridge.
abe: Abe no Hirafu! General of the cold northern sea! / A hundred and eighty ships against the Emishi, and I caught Mishihase arrows in my teeth! Tang’s next! Ha!
boksin: You’re not on the board, Admiral. / …Lovely entrance, though.
Echi no Takutsu waits until the admiral has finished, which takes a while. Then he walks up the shingle, turns his back on the Baekje generals and bows to the sea he has just crossed, low and long, the tails of his white headband lifting in the wind, before he turns round and says the one thing he has prepared.
takutsu: No one in this country knows my name. So instead of mine, I will say yours. / Long live Kudara. If Kudara needs a life, begin with mine.
sateksangya: …He means it.
Dochim introduces himself sitting down. He has found a flat rock above the tideline and settled on it in his red kasaya, the beads running through one hand and the gilt staff across his knees, and he smiles at the new king the way a monk smiles at a donor whose gift has not yet arrived.
dochim: Dochim. A monk of no temple, now. They call me General of the Spirit Army. / The Buddha taught that all things are impermanent. The Tang garrison at Sabi is one of those things. / We march at dawn. Do sleep well tonight.
Boksin, who did not write “General of the Spirit Army” on the board, makes a small mark beside it.
Heukchi Sangji is seven feet tall. The autumn Sabi fell he walked into Imjon with a handful of men and walked out ten days later with thirty thousand, and he regards the whole business of a roll call as a kind of weather. When his turn comes he steps forward exactly one pace.
sangji: Heukchi Sangji. Imjon. / …That’s it.
boksin: The arms, General. We discussed the arms.
sangji: You discussed the arms.
Satek Sangya has worn the tall gilt cap of his house for the occasion, which is the only concession he makes to it. He does not look up from the ledger.
sateksangya: Satek Sangya. Forty boats, eleven hundred bales of rice, thirty thousand arrows, and I stopped counting the rope. / Nobody has paid me yet. That’s my pose.
Then Gwishil Boksin, who wrote the board, steps out in front of all of them, plants the red shaft in the shingle and does the arms exactly as rehearsed.
boksin: Gwishil Boksin. I raised this country once when it fell, and if it falls twice I’ll raise it twice. / Welcome home, Majesty. Your army.
Everyone looks at the king. Nobody has given Pung a line. He has been in the country for less than an hour and has spent most of it being bowed at, and he ad-libs.
pung: I am Buyeo Pung, son of King Euija, and… king of— of Baekje. / …Is that right? Is “restoration” the word?
boksin: Close enough, Majesty.
Boksin counts them in. “Baekje— Restoration— Army!” Takutsu and the admiral land it perfectly, which is embarrassing for everyone else. Dochim does half and goes back to his beads. Sangya is still counting. Sangji folds his arms, which is at least an arm. The new king is a beat late and on the wrong foot.
They try it twice more before supper. For the second, Boksin puts the king on a rock in the middle so that everyone is at least pointing at the same man, and Abe lifts Sangji off the ground to make the shape symmetrical, which nobody asked for and Sangji does not forgive. For the third, Dochim declines to stand, Sangya sits down on the rice, and the king, finally, gets the arms right, a beat after everyone else has stopped.
On the far ridge two Tang scouts watch the whole performance, and that night Liu Rengui files their report under morale.
The crown is Pung’s. The army is Boksin’s. Everyone can see the arithmetic of that, including both of them.
[FLASHBACK 643 The year after Daeya]
  chunchu: Daeya did not fall because a wall came down. / A door was opened from the inside.
  yushin: You mean to suspect an entire country because of one Gumil.
  chunchu: No. / I mean every country has a Gumil in it. / We had ours. / So find Baekje’s. Find Goguryeo’s. And if it comes to it, find the Tang’s.
  It takes eleven years. A captured Silla servant named Jomi-gon is sent back into Baekje as a household man to the minister Imja, and spends years being useful, and one evening asks a question he has been carrying since he left.
  jomigon: My lord. / When the country falls, what becomes of your house?
  Imja does not report the question, which is the answer.
Boksin and Pung will not need a Gumil. They will do it to each other unassisted, which Chunchu also predicted, in a sentence his son has written down and kept.
Chunchu had put it in a sentence his son kept — not a line from the annals, only counsel: where blood ties are strong, the state grows weak.
Pung was the only prince left, so they crowned him. Boksin did the crowning. Boksin is starting to regret it.
Boksin, the lead general of the Revival Society, commands its armies — and begins to resent the king he crowned.
Boksin sends a messenger to the Tang walls with a question.
boksin: When are you gentlemen going home, Ambassador? / Name the day. We’d like to see you off properly.
liurengui: Tell him we are guests. / Guests leave when the host can keep his own house. This host has two kings, one army and no roof. We’ll stay for dinner.
Then Prince Pung wants to move house. The hill is barren, he says. The people will starve. Down on the plain there is rice.
After 2 months, they’re forced to move back because it is too close to the Silla border.
pung: This Juryu lies far from farmland, its soil barren and unfit for farming or sericulture; it is good ground for defence and for battle. If we stay long the people will starve — better now to move to Pisong. Pisong has the Goryeondangyeong running about it like a sash to the northwest, and to the southeast deep marshes and great embankments; ringed with earth, and when the sluices are opened the water pours forth. The produce of its flowering and fruiting trees will be the richest in all Samhan, and the source of clothing and food lies hidden between heaven and earth there. Low ground it may be — but why should we not move?
takutsu: Pisong lies a single night’s march from the enemy. So close that if the unexpected comes, regret will be useless. Starving is a later matter; ruin comes first. The reason the enemy does not come freely now is that Juryu sits in rough mountains — every slope a defence, the peaks high and the valleys narrow, easy to hold and hard to attack. If we sit on low ground, how shall we stand firm, and how shall we last until today’s tomorrow?
The men move once, move back, and start looking at each other differently.
Baekje has its king back. Now the emperor turns north, to walls that have never fallen…!
